node-1.label: Patient had a pruritic and painful periorbital eruption lasting 1 month

node-2.label: Medical history included lupus nephritis requiring hemodialysis, immune thrombocytopenia, acute myeloid leukemia, chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy, deep vein thrombosis, diverticulitis, and postcolectomy diarrhea.

node-3.label: Past treatments included hydroxychloroquine (resulted in retinal toxic effects) and lenalidomide (severely worsened platelet count, with a nadir of 28 ×103/μL).

node-4.label: Physical examination demonstrated scaly, crusted pink plaques that involved the periorbital skin.

attrs.why: Both the pathologist and laboratory physician analyses highlight the left upper eyelid biopsy showing vacuolar interface dermatitis with follicular involvement and epidermal atrophy—a classic histologic pattern of cutaneous lupus. Combined with the established autoimmune background (lupus nephritis/ITP) and the scaly crusted periorbital plaques, this new biopsy evidence strengthens the diagnosis, so confidence is raised from 0.7 to 0.75. It is not higher because DIF and autoantibody testing remain unavailable.

The newly available biopsy demonstrating vacuolar interface dermatitis with follicular involvement and epidermal atrophy is the histologic hallmark of cutaneous lupus rather than a drug-induced eruption. The lenalidomide/hydroxychloroquine exposure remains only circumstantial and the medication timing is unconfirmed, so the drug-eruption hypothesis is weakened and confidence reduced from 0.2 to 0.1.

The new biopsy findings (vacuolar interface dermatitis with follicular involvement and epidermal atrophy) are not the histologic pattern expected in seborrheic dermatitis, which typically shows spongiosis and parakeratosis without interface change. Immunosuppression and the periorbital plaques still allow it as a remote possibility, but confidence is lowered from 0.1 to 0.05.
